en: The placid banks of the Ipiranga heard
the resounding cry of a heroic people.
And the sun of Liberty, in flashing rays,
shone in the sky of the Homeland at that instant.
If the pledge of this equality
we have managed to win with a strong arm,
in your bosom, O Liberty,
our breast defies death itself!
O beloved Homeland,
idolized,
hail! Hail!
Brazil, an intense dream, a vivid ray
of love and of hope descends to the earth,
if in your beautiful sky, smiling and clear,
the image of the Southern Cross shines resplendent.
A giant by your very nature,
you are beautiful, you are strong, a fearless colossus,
and your future mirrors that greatness,
Adored land,
among a thousand others
it is you, Brazil,
O beloved Homeland!
Of the children of this soil
you are the gentle mother,
beloved Homeland,
Brazil!
Lying eternally in a splendid cradle,
to the sound of the sea and in the light of the deep sky,
you shine, O Brazil, flower-ornament of America,
lit by the sun of the New World!
Than the most gaily adorned land
your smiling, lovely fields have more flowers;
"our woods have more life,"
"our life" in your bosom "more loves."
O beloved Homeland,
idolized,
hail! Hail!
Brazil, of eternal love may it be the symbol,
the starry banner that you display,
and may the green-and-gold of this pennant say:
— Peace in the future and glory in the past.
But if you raise the strong club of justice,
you will see that a son of yours does not flee from the fight,
nor does one who adores you fear death itself,
Adored land,
among a thousand others
it is you, Brazil,
O beloved Homeland!
Of the children of this soil
you are the gentle mother,
beloved Homeland,
Brazil!
notes: lines 1.1-1.2: the order of the original is 'Heard, from the Ipiranga, the placid banks / of a heroic people the resounding cry'; the subject is 'the placid banks', the object 'the resounding cry'.
lines 2.1-2.4: 'penhor' is a pledge or guarantee. In line 2.4 the subject is 'o nosso peito' (our breast) and the object 'a própria morte' (death itself).
line 4.3: 'Se' is 'if', here with the sense 'when' or 'since'.
line 4.4: 'o Cruzeiro' is the constellation of the Southern Cross ('Cruzeiro do Sul').
lines 5.3 and 12.3 end with a comma in the original: the sentence runs on into the following 'Adored land' stanza.
line 8.3: 'florão' is a large flower-shaped ornament, a rosette; figuratively the pride or jewel of something.
line 9.1: 'garrida' is 'showy, elegant, brightly adorned'; the line compares Brazil's fields with those of the most gaily adorned land.
lines 9.3-9.4: the words in quotation marks are quoted from Gonçalves Dias's poem 'Canção do exílio'; line 9.4 reads in full 'our life in your bosom [has] more loves'.
line 11.2: 'lábaro' is a banner or standard (from the Roman labarum).
line 11.3: 'verde-louro' is read as 'green and gold' ('louro' = blond, golden-yellow); 'louro' also means 'laurel', so it can be taken as 'laurel-green'.
line 12.1: 'clava' is a club or mace.
